name: Estonia
traditionNote: A Germanic civil-law system rebuilt from scratch after 1991 and unusually digital: the binding rule is the enacted text in Riigi Teataja, which is not merely online but online-only, digitally sealed, and browsable at any date in the past or the future.
summary: Acts (seadus) are passed by the 101-member Riigikogu and proclaimed by the President, who may instead refuse proclamation and send the act back or ask the Supreme Court to rule on its constitutionality. An act takes effect on the tenth day after publication in Riigi Teataja unless it says otherwise, which is the constitutional default in § 108. Regulations (määrus) are issued by the Government and by individual ministers only on the strength of an authorisation in an act, and orders (korraldus) settle single cases. Everything is published in Riigi Teataja, which since 2010 exists only as an electronic edition — there is no printed gazette to fall back on, and each published text carries a digital seal. The gazette runs in four parts: RT I for legislative acts, RT II for treaties, RT III for individual acts of the Riigikogu, the President and the Government, and RT IV for the regulations of the 79 local authorities. Estonia has no separate constitutional court; constitutional review is exercised by the Constitutional Review Chamber of the Riigikohus, which can be reached by the President, the Chancellor of Justice, a local council, or any court that refuses to apply a provision it considers unconstitutional.
hierarchy: Eesti Vabariigi põhiseadus (Constitution, 1992) read together with the 2003 Constitution Amendment Act, which conditions the Constitution on Estonia's EU membership
EU law (directly applicable regulations; directives implemented by Estonian acts)
Välislepingud — treaties ratified by the Riigikogu, ranking above conflicting acts
Vabariigi Valitsuse määrus — Government regulations issued under an authorisation in an act
Ministri määrus — ministerial regulations, likewise only on a statutory authorisation
Kohaliku omavalitsuse volikogu ja valitsuse määrus — local council and local government regulations, published in RT IV

gazette.name: Riigi Teataja
gazette.authority: Justiits- ja Digiministeerium (Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs); operated by Registrite ja Infosüsteemide Keskus
gazette.coverage: Continuous from 1918, with the 1918-1944 gazette kept as a separate historical collection; electronic-only publication since 2010, updated on publication days through the week
gazette.desc: The one place an Estonian legal act acquires force. Published in four parts — RT I legislative acts, RT II treaties, RT III individual acts of the Riigikogu, President and Government, RT IV local authority regulations — and unusually, it carries both the text as adopted and a consolidated text for every date the act has had, so 'what did this section say in March 2019' is a date field rather than a research project.
gazette.howto: The front page lists what was published in each part on each of the last five publication days, under 'Ilmumas ja ilmunud'. From the top menu, Terviktekstid gives consolidated texts, Algtekstid the texts as adopted, Välislepingud treaties, Kohtuteave court information, Eelnõud pending bills and Tõlked translations. Every act page carries its publication mark in the form 'RT I, 11.04.2025, 3', which is the citation you quote.
gazette.note: Only the Estonian text has legal force. Riigi Teataja states plainly that its English translations do not, and cannot be relied on in judicial or other official proceedings.

constitution.name: Eesti Vabariigi pohiseadus
constitution.en: Constitution of the Republic of Estonia
constitution.authority: Adopted by referendum 28 June 1992; published and maintained in Riigi Teataja
constitution.coverage: In force since 3 July 1992, amended in 2003, 2007, 2011, 2015 and again in 2025; Riigi Teataja shows the wording in force on any chosen date
constitution.desc: A short constitution of fifteen chapters, supplemented rather than rewritten by the Constitution Amendment Act carried at the 2003 EU referendum, which is why Estonian constitutional law is read as the 1992 text plus that act. The Riigi Teataja page carries the current wording, every earlier wording, and links across to the commented edition, the Constitutional Assembly materials and the Supreme Court's own analyses.
constitution.howto: The '?leiaKehtiv' suffix on any Riigi Teataja act URL jumps from an old version to the wording currently in force — a stale link cannot silently show you a repealed text. Use 'Ajatelg' for the timeline of versions, 'Võrdle' to diff two wordings and 'Võrdle tõlkega' to set the Estonian against the English. The English text sits at riigiteataja.ee/en/eli/521052015001/consolide.
constitution.note: Amendments may be made by referendum, by two successive compositions of the Riigikogu, or as a matter of urgency by a four-fifths majority; there is no eternity clause but §§ 1, 2, 3(1) and chapters I and XV can only be amended by referendum.

sources.name: Terviktekstid (Riigi Teataja)
sources.authority: Justiits- ja Digiministeerium / Registrite ja Infosüsteemide Keskus
sources.coverage: Every act and regulation in force, each with the full series of its earlier wordings; the default search date is today, and any past or future date can be substituted
sources.desc: The working text of Estonian law: an act with its amendments merged in, published by the state rather than by an editor, and versioned so completely that the consolidated text is itself part of the official gazette rather than a convenience copy of it.
sources.howto: Search by title, by text or by an act's abbreviation — 'PS' finds the Constitution. The advanced panel on the left filters by issuer and type of act, by ministers' regulations, by acts published together with a treaty, and by local authority, including a 'Vali kaardilt' option that picks the municipality off a map. 'Kehtivuse kuupäev' sets the date whose wording you want; 'Kehtivuse ajavahemik' finds everything in force across a period.
sources.note: Consolidated texts here are official, not editorial — but check the version date shown at the head of the text, because a search can legitimately return a wording that is not the current one.

sources.name: Algtekstid (Riigi Teataja)
sources.authority: Justiits- ja Digiministeerium / Registrite ja Infosüsteemide Keskus
sources.coverage: Acts and regulations as they were published on the day they were published, back through the electronic era and the printed gazette
sources.desc: The as-enacted record, separate from the consolidated one. An amending act is a document in its own right here: this is where you read what a 2019 amendment actually said, rather than the trace it left in the amended act.
sources.howto: Search by title or number, or work from the 'Ilmumas ja ilmunud' lists on the front page, which are organised by RT part and publication date. Each consolidated text also links back to the original text it grew out of, and to every amending act, under 'Muudetud järgmiste aktidega'.
sources.note: 'Seaduste kokkuvõtted' in the same menu gives plain-language summaries of newly passed acts — a summary, not a text, and not something to cite.

sources.name: Riigi Teataja English translations
sources.authority: Justiits- ja Digiministeerium, translations made by sworn translators
sources.coverage: Consolidated English texts of acts in force, from the launch of the English site on 31 October 2013 onward; a MY RT subscription notifies you by e-mail when a translation is updated
sources.desc: Estonia translates far more of its legislation than most civil-law states, and keeps the translations consolidated rather than frozen at the date of enactment. It remains a translation service: the site says so on its own introduction page.
sources.howto: Search the English site directly, or open any Estonian act and take 'Tõlge inglise keelde'. On an English act page, 'Open authentic text' and 'Compare with authentic' put the Estonian beside it — the fastest way to check whether a translated phrase is carrying the weight you think it is.
sources.note: Translations have no legal force and cannot be relied on in proceedings; in Estonia legislation has legal force only in Estonian. Ukrainian and Russian collections are separate and much smaller.

sources.name: Valislepingud (Riigi Teataja)
sources.authority: Välisministeerium (Ministry of Foreign Affairs); published in RT II
sources.coverage: Treaties binding on Estonia, published in RT II with their ratification acts and entry-into-force notices
sources.desc: Treaties rank above ordinary acts under § 123 of the Constitution, so this is not a diplomatic archive but part of the operative hierarchy. Ratified treaties are published in RT II together with the act that ratified them and the notice fixing the date they entered into force.
sources.howto: Search by title or by party; 'Välislepingute liigitus poolte alusel' sorts the collection by counterparty, and 'Terviktekstid koos välislepinguga' finds domestic acts published together with a treaty. The Foreign Ministry's own page on treaty publication explains which instruments go to RT II and when.

sources.name: Kohtuteave (Riigi Teataja)
sources.authority: Registrite ja Infosüsteemide Keskus, publishing decisions supplied by the courts
sources.coverage: Decisions of the county, administrative, circuit and supreme courts that have entered into force, with summaries; plus hearing times and places, and summaries of European Court of Human Rights judgments concerning Estonia
sources.desc: The national case-law search, sitting inside the gazette rather than beside it — which means a decision can be reached from the provision it interprets and vice versa. Estonia publishes entered-into-force judgments across all instances, not only the supreme ones.
sources.howto: Enter a case number in 'Lahendi number', or use the separate searches for decision summaries, for hearing times and places, and for the publication of decisions. From any consolidated act, the 'Kohtulahendid' tab lists the decisions citing it; 'sätte ajalugu' and 'kohtulahendid' in the relation buttons narrow that to a single section.
sources.note: Personal data in published judgments is restricted under the courts' rules, so names may appear as initials or be replaced.

sources.name: Riigikohus
sources.coverage: Decisions of the civil, criminal, administrative and constitutional review chambers, the Special Panel and the full court (üldkogu), with the court's own analyses of its practice
sources.desc: Estonia's court of last instance and, sitting as the Constitutional Review Chamber, its constitutional court — there is no separate one. It reviews acts for conformity with the Constitution on application from the President, the Chancellor of Justice, a local council or a lower court that has refused to apply a provision.
sources.howto: Take 'Lahendid' for decisions and 'Menetlus Riigikohtus' for how a matter reaches the court, including what makes an appeal in cassation admissible. The court's analyses of its own case law sit under its documents section, and the site also runs in English, Russian and French.
sources.note: The full text of a Supreme Court decision is also in the Riigi Teataja court-decision search, which is usually the faster route if you already have a citation.

sources.name: Riigikogu eelnoud
sources.coverage: Bills initiated, taken into proceedings, pending and completed, with explanatory memoranda, committee documents, readings and amendment deadlines
sources.desc: Where a bill is followed through its three readings. The seletuskiri — the explanatory memorandum attached to a bill — is the standard Estonian travaux préparatoire and is routinely relied on when a provision is ambiguous.
sources.howto: Search by bill title or number, or use the quick links for 'Algatatud eelnõud', 'Menetlusse võetud eelnõud' and 'Menetletud eelnõud'; the list can be sorted by number, title, date of change and status, and filtered by reading. Deadlines for tabling amendments are listed under 'Muudatusettepanekute tähtajad'.
sources.note: A bill's file here ends at adoption; the published act is in Riigi Teataja, which is also where the pending-bills view under 'Eelnõud' links back to.

sources.name: Eelnoude infosusteem (EIS)
sources.coverage: Drafts circulating between ministries for coordination and public consultation, before they reach the Government or the Riigikogu
sources.desc: The stage before a bill exists as a bill. Ministries put draft acts and regulations here for inter-ministerial approval and for comment, with the explanatory memorandum, the impact assessment and the responses attached — the earliest point at which a rule that will affect you is visible.
sources.howto: Browse or search the drafts, then open a file to see its coordination round, the deadline for comments and the opinions already submitted. Government regulations, which never pass through Parliament, are often visible here and nowhere else until they are published.
sources.note: A draft here is not law and may change beyond recognition or be dropped; nothing in this system is citable as a rule.

sources.name: Kohaliku omavalitsuse maarused (RT IV)
sources.authority: The 79 local authorities; published centrally in Riigi Teataja part IV
sources.coverage: Regulations of city and rural municipal councils and governments, consolidated the same way as national acts
sources.desc: Estonia does something few states do: it publishes municipal legislation in the national gazette, in consolidated and versioned form. Building rules, waste rules, school catchment rules and local taxes are all in the same system and the same search as an act of the Riigikogu.
sources.howto: Use the subject classification for local regulations, or the consolidated-text search with the 'Kohaliku omavalitsuse määrused' filter — 'Vali kaardilt' lets you pick the municipality from a map if you know the place but not its official name.
sources.note: Individual decisions of a council (otsus) are not regulations and are not all published here; those are held by the local authority itself.

sources.name: Ametlikud Teadaanded
sources.authority: Justiits- ja Digiministeerium / Registrite ja Infosüsteemide Keskus
sources.coverage: Notices required by law to be published officially, current and archived, with a separate view of insolvency data
sources.desc: The notice gazette, distinct from Riigi Teataja: bankruptcy and insolvency notices, summonses, auctions, liquidations of public-law bodies, professional competitions, declarations of death or disappearance, and the rest of the machinery that has to happen in public. No legislation is published here.
sources.howto: Search all notices, or restrict to insolvency data with the checkbox; the advanced search filters by notice type from a long list of categories. The 'Andmete taaskasutamine' section covers bulk reuse of the data.
sources.note: Publication here has legal consequences — deadlines often run from the date of the notice — but a notice is never a source of law.

sources.name: Oiguskantsler
sources.authority: Õiguskantsleri Kantselei (Office of the Chancellor of Justice)
sources.coverage: Opinions, memoranda and annual reports; proposals to the Riigikogu to bring legislation into conformity with the Constitution, and applications to the Supreme Court
sources.desc: An office with no clear equivalent elsewhere: an independent official who reviews legislation for constitutionality, acts as ombudsman, and can take an act to the Supreme Court. Its opinions are the closest thing Estonia has to a running constitutional commentary on new legislation.
sources.howto: Browse the opinions by subject or search by keyword; each item states the provision at issue and the outcome. Where the Chancellor has asked the Riigikogu to change a provision, the file usually names the act and section, which is the fastest route into the constitutional argument about it.
sources.note: An opinion of the Chancellor binds nobody. It is persuasive, frequently followed, and occasionally the first step towards a provision being struck down.

sources.name: Pohiseaduse kommenteeritud valjaanne
sources.authority: Sihtasutus Iuridicum, with an editorial board of Estonian constitutional lawyers
sources.coverage: Every section of the Constitution, the Constitution Implementation Act and the Constitution Amendment Act, with a bibliography and subject index
sources.desc: The standard commentary on the Estonian Constitution, section by section, free to read online. Estonian constitutional argument is conducted largely through it, and the Riigi Teataja page for the Constitution links to it directly.
sources.howto: Open a chapter from the sidebar and read down to the section you need, or use the subject index (Märksõnastik); each commentary cites the Supreme Court decisions on that section.
sources.note: Scholarship, not an official text. Where it disagrees with the Supreme Court, the Supreme Court governs.

sources.name: Jurist aitab
sources.en: Legal aid portal, with Russian texts of legislation
sources.authority: Justiits- ja Digiministeerium, operated under contract by Eesti Juristide Liit
sources.coverage: Russian translations of selected acts, alongside plain-language legal information and a free advice service
sources.desc: Where the Russian-language texts of Estonian legislation live — Riigi Teataja links out to here rather than hosting them. The selection is oriented to everyday law: family, employment, tenancy, social benefits, procedure.
sources.howto: Open the legislation section and pick the act; the same site carries explanatory articles and a question service in Russian and Estonian.
sources.note: Translations, with the same standing as the English ones: none. Only the Estonian text in Riigi Teataja has legal force.

sources.name: EUR-Lex (eesti keeles)
sources.authority: Euroopa Liidu Väljaannete Talitus (Publications Office of the European Union)
sources.coverage: EU treaties, legislation, consolidated texts, case law and national implementing measures, in Estonian among the official languages
sources.desc: A substantial part of the law applied in Estonia is EU law, which Riigi Teataja does not carry. Regulations apply without an Estonian act; directives are traceable to the Estonian acts notified as implementing them.
sources.howto: Search by CELEX number or subject with the interface set to Estonian; the national implementing measures tab on a directive lists the Estonian acts notified for it. Riigi Teataja's own menu links out to the consolidated EUR-Lex texts and to the transposition overview kept by the Government Office.
sources.note: The Estonian language version of an EU act is authentic alongside the others, but the Official Journal edition is the binding one.

findLaw.task: Find the current text of an act
findLaw.steps: Search the consolidated texts by title or by the act's abbreviation, and open it. Check the version header — 'Kehtiv sõnastus' with a date means you are on the wording in force. If you arrived from an old link, append '?leiaKehtiv' to the URL and Riigi Teataja will move you to the current version.

findLaw.task: Read the law as it stood on a particular date
findLaw.steps: Set 'Kehtivuse kuupäev' in the advanced search to the date you care about, or open the act and use 'Ajatelg' to pick a version from the timeline. 'Võrdle' puts two wordings side by side so you can see exactly what an amendment changed.

findLaw.task: See the amendment itself, not its effect
findLaw.steps: Open the act and expand 'Muudetud järgmiste aktidega' to list every amending act with its publication mark, then open the amending act in the original-texts collection to read what it actually enacted, including transitional provisions that never appear in the consolidated text.

findLaw.task: Find a court decision, or the decisions on a section
findLaw.steps: Search by case number in the Riigi Teataja court-decision search, or open the act and take the 'Kohtulahendid' tab to see the decisions citing it — the relation buttons narrow that to a single section. Supreme Court decisions and the court's analyses are also on riigikohus.ee.

Use the consolidated-text search filtered to local authority regulations, picking the municipality from the list or from the map. Estonian municipal regulations are published in Riigi Teataja part IV and consolidated like national ones, so the same date and version tools apply.

findLaw.task: Read an Estonian act in English
findLaw.steps: Search the English site, or open the Estonian act and take 'Tõlge inglise keelde'. Translations are consolidated rather than frozen, but check the date on the English text and use 'Compare with authentic' before relying on any phrase — the English has no legal force at all.

findLaw.task: Follow a rule that has not been made yet
findLaw.steps: For bills, use the Riigikogu's proceedings pages, where each bill carries its explanatory memorandum and reading dates. For drafts still inside government — including regulations that never go to Parliament — look in the Government Office's draft information system, which shows the coordination round and the comments received.

subnational: Estonia is a unitary state with a single tier of local government: 79 city and rural municipalities, whose councils adopt regulations (määrus) within the powers given them by act. What is unusual is where those regulations live — since local government legislation was brought into the state gazette, they are published as part IV of Riigi Teataja and consolidated and versioned exactly like national acts, searchable in the same interface and selectable from a map. There are no regions, states or provinces with legislative power, and no minority-language legal regime: county governments were abolished in 2017 and their functions divided between the state and the municipalities.
caveats: Only the Estonian text has legal force. Riigi Teataja's own introduction says its English translations do not have legal force and cannot be relied on in judicial or other proceedings, and the same is true of the Russian texts on Jurist aitab; translations are consolidated but can still trail the Estonian. Because every act carries versions for every date it has had, a link found in a search or a document can perfectly legitimately point at a wording that has been superseded — read the version header, and use '?leiaKehtiv' to jump to the wording in force. Drafts in the Government Office system and bills before the Riigikogu are not law and change; the commented edition of the Constitution is scholarship and the Chancellor of Justice's opinions bind nobody. Court decisions are published with personal data restricted, so a judgment may name parties only by initials. Finally, Riigi Teataja carries no EU legislation: for a regulation that applies in Estonia without any Estonian act, EUR-Lex is the source.
